title: Lithium tried for mania in Melbourne
summary: In 1949 the psychiatrist John Cade reported that lithium salts calmed patients with mania at a veterans' hospital in Melbourne, reviving a forgotten substance as a psychiatric treatment.
explanation:
John Cade was working at the Bundoora Repatriation Hospital, a veterans' hospital on the edge of Melbourne, when he began experiments based on a theory that mania might be caused by a toxic substance in the body. Giving lithium salts to laboratory animals, he noticed that they became calmer.

He then gave lithium citrate and lithium carbonate to ten patients with mania. Several improved strikingly, and he published the results in the Medical Journal of Australia in 1949. Lithium had been used in medicine in the nineteenth century, but its psychiatric use had been forgotten.

Cade's report was an uncontrolled case series. In Denmark, Mogens Schou tested lithium for mania in a trial that allocated patients to lithium or placebo, published in 1954. Uptake was uneven: the United States approved lithium only in 1970, becoming the 50th country to do so.

whyItMattered: Lithium remains a standard treatment for bipolar disorder, and Cade's report helped open the era of psychiatric drug treatment.
limitations: Cade's ten patients were not compared with a control group; firmer evidence came from later controlled trials.
His original theory about a toxin causing mania was not borne out.

title: Artemisinin extracted from qinghao
summary: Working within China's secret national malaria programme, Project 523, Tu Youyou's group found that a low-temperature extract of qinghao (Artemisia annua) cleared malaria parasites in animals in 1971 and in patients in 1972.
explanation:
In the 1960s Chinese military institutes began confidential research on drugs against malaria, and in 1967 a national office was set up to coordinate the work, known as Project 523. In 1969 Tu Youyou, at the Institute of Chinese Materia Medica in Beijing, was appointed to lead a group searching traditional Chinese medicine for candidates.

Early extracts of qinghao gave inconsistent results. A passage in Ge Hong's Handbook of Prescriptions for Emergencies describes soaking the herb in cold water and wringing out the juice, rather than boiling it. Suspecting that heat destroyed the active ingredient, Tu's group changed to low-temperature extraction. On 4 October 1971, sample 191, an ether extract, completely inhibited malaria parasites in rodents.

Between August and October 1972 the extract was tested on 21 patients in Hainan, all of whom lost their fever and parasites, and on further patients in Beijing. Other institutions helped determine the structure of the active compound, artemisinin. Artemisinin-based combination therapies later became the standard treatment for falciparum malaria worldwide.

title: Stomach ulcers traced to a bacterium
summary: In Perth, the pathologist Robin Warren and the physician Barry Marshall showed that curved bacteria, later named Helicobacter pylori, live in the stomach and cause gastritis and most peptic ulcers.
explanation:
Robin Warren noticed small curved bacteria on stomach biopsies, in the lower part of the stomach of about half of patients examined, always alongside inflammation. Together with Barry Marshall, he set out to test the link. After several failed attempts, Marshall succeeded in growing the bacterium in culture in 1982.

At the time, stress and lifestyle were considered the main causes of peptic ulcer, and the idea that bacteria could survive in the acid stomach met resistance. Marshall and Warren went on to show that the bacterium causes gastritis and peptic ulcer disease.

Peptic ulcer disease, often chronic and recurrent, became curable with a short course of antibiotics and acid-reducing drugs.

title: The virus that causes AIDS is isolated
summary: In 1983 Françoise Barré-Sinoussi, Luc Montagnier and colleagues at the Institut Pasteur isolated a new retrovirus from the lymph node of a patient at risk of AIDS. It became known as HIV.
explanation:
By the early 1980s many researchers suspected that AIDS had an infectious cause, and the Paris team decided to test whether it might be a retrovirus. The Paris team cultured lymph node cells from patients with swollen lymph glands and early signs of immune damage, and detected a new retrovirus, which they called lymphadenopathy-associated virus (LAV), publishing in Science in 1983.

In 1984, Robert Gallo's group at the US National Institutes of Health reported a virus from many patients, named HTLV-III, and Jay Levy's group in San Francisco separately identified a related virus. The viruses proved to be the same, and in 1985 an international committee named it human immunodeficiency virus.

Identifying the virus led to blood tests that protected blood supplies and allowed diagnosis, and to antiretroviral drugs. Combination therapy greatly extended life expectancy where it was available; the drugs suppress the virus but do not cure the infection.

title: Modified mRNA, from a 2005 finding to COVID-19 vaccines
summary: Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman found in 2005 that chemically modified building blocks stop synthetic mRNA from triggering inflammation. Their work enabled the mRNA vaccines against COVID-19 approved in December 2020.
explanation:
Using messenger RNA to make the body produce a vaccine antigen had been proposed decades earlier, but synthetic mRNA provoked inflammation and produced little protein. Working at the University of Pennsylvania, Karikó and Weissman showed that immune cells treat unmodified synthetic mRNA as foreign, and that changing its nucleoside bases almost abolished the reaction. They published in 2005; later studies showed that modified mRNA also produces much more protein.

When the SARS-CoV-2 pandemic began, this groundwork, combined with other advances and very large public and private investment, allowed two base-modified mRNA vaccines to be developed and tested at unprecedented speed. Both were approved in December 2020, with reported protection of around 95% against disease in their trials.

whatChanged: Made mRNA usable as a vaccine platform by removing its inflammatory effect and increasing protein production.
whyItMattered: Enabled highly effective COVID-19 vaccines within a year of the pandemic's start, and a platform now applied to other diseases.
limitations: The 2020 vaccines also depended on other advances, including lipid delivery and stabilised spike proteins.
Global access to COVID-19 vaccines was very unequal, especially in 2021.

title: Smallpox eradicated
summary: After an intensified WHO-led campaign launched in 1967, the last natural case of smallpox occurred in Merca, Somalia, in October 1977. In May 1980 the World Health Assembly declared the disease eradicated.
explanation:
Smallpox had afflicted humanity for at least 3,000 years and, by WHO's estimate, killed some 300 million people in the twentieth century alone. In 1967 the World Health Organization launched an intensified eradication programme, which worked by identifying every case and its contacts and making sure they were vaccinated. Within four years the disease was gone from Latin America; four more years ended it in Asia.

The final naturally acquired case was Ali Maow Maalin, a 23-year-old hospital cook and former vaccinator in Merca, Somalia, who fell ill after guiding a vehicle carrying two infected children in October 1977. He recovered and later worked in Somalia's polio eradication campaign.

After two years of searching for any remaining transmission, an independent Global Commission certified eradication in December 1979, and on 8 May 1980 the World Health Assembly formally declared it. A laboratory accident in Birmingham, England, in 1978 caused the last known cases and one death.

title: First malaria vaccine recommended for children
summary: On 6 October 2021 WHO recommended broad use of the RTS,S/AS01 malaria vaccine for children in areas with moderate to high transmission, based on a pilot programme in Ghana, Kenya and Malawi.
explanation:
From 2019, the health ministries of Ghana, Kenya and Malawi introduced the RTS,S vaccine into routine childhood immunisation in selected areas, as a pilot coordinated by WHO. By the time of the recommendation, the programme had reached more than 800,000 children.

After reviewing two years of data on safety, feasibility and impact, WHO's advisory bodies recommended the vaccine for children in sub-Saharan Africa and other regions with moderate to high transmission of Plasmodium falciparum. It was the first vaccine recommended against any human parasitic disease. A second vaccine, R21/Matrix-M, was recommended in October 2023.

WHO presents the vaccine as an addition to existing tools such as bed nets and prompt treatment, not a replacement for them.

title: Random allocation tests streptomycin for tuberculosis
summary: A Medical Research Council trial published in 1948 assigned patients with pulmonary tuberculosis to streptomycin or to usual care without it using random numbers held in sealed envelopes. It became a model for the randomised controlled trial.
explanation:
When the antibiotic streptomycin became available, the British Medical Research Council organised a trial in several hospitals. The statistician Austin Bradford Hill designed a scheme in which each patient's allocation was decided by random numbers, kept in sealed envelopes marked only with the hospital's name and a number, so that clinicians could not influence who received the drug.

The trial, reported in the British Medical Journal in 1948, found a markedly lower death rate among patients given streptomycin. Its lasting importance lay in its method: concealed random allocation protects comparisons from the conscious and unconscious choices of those running a trial.

Historians note that allocation by alternation had been used in earlier controlled trials, and that the word 'random' sometimes appeared in earlier reports when alternation was actually used.

title: Insulin first treats a dying boy in Toronto
summary: In 1921–22 a University of Toronto team extracted insulin from the pancreas. On 23 January 1922 a purified extract brought 14-year-old Leonard Thompson's diabetes under control, turning a fatal disease into a treatable one.
explanation:
Type 1 diabetes was then a universally fatal disease. In the summer of 1921 Frederick Banting and Charles Best, working in J. J. R. Macleod's laboratory, showed that a pancreatic extract lowered blood sugar in diabetic dogs. Early presentations did not convince everyone, since earlier investigators had reported similar effects without producing a usable treatment.

On 11 January 1922 Leonard Thompson, a 14-year-old near death at Toronto General Hospital, was injected with Banting and Best's extract. It lowered his blood sugar but had little clinical effect. The biochemist James Collip then produced a purer extract, and from 23 January Thompson improved dramatically. He lived another 13 years.

Production was scaled up with the university's Connaught Laboratories and drug companies, and the Nobel Prize of 1923 went to two members of the team, Banting and Macleod, amid lasting disputes over credit.

title: Penicillin: from a mould in London to mass production
summary: Alexander Fleming noticed in 1928 that a Penicillium mould killed bacteria. A decade later Howard Florey, Ernst Chain and their Oxford team showed it could treat infections, and wartime research in the United States made mass production possible.
explanation:
Returning from holiday in September 1928, Fleming found a culture plate at St Mary's Hospital in London where bacteria had failed to grow around a contaminating mould. He identified it as Penicillium and showed it killed many disease-causing bacteria, but the substance was hard to produce and remained a laboratory curiosity.

From 1939, Florey, Chain, Norman Heatley and others at Oxford developed ways to extract it and showed that it protected infected mice. In 1941 an Oxford police constable became the first person treated; he improved but died when supplies ran out.

With Britain at war, production research moved to the United States, including the Department of Agriculture laboratory in Peoria, Illinois, and drug companies that developed deep-tank fermentation. Penicillin was produced at scale from 1944. Fleming, Florey and Chain shared the 1945 Nobel Prize.

title: Oral rehydration: sugar and salt water against cholera
summary: Trials in Dhaka in 1968 showed that a solution of glucose and salt taken by mouth could replace much of the intravenous fluid needed in cholera. In 1971, in refugee camps during the Bangladesh Liberation War, Dilip Mahalanabis showed it worked even where families gave it themselves.
explanation:
Untreated cholera killed 30–40 per cent of patients, and intravenous fluids, the only effective treatment, were difficult and costly to provide in large outbreaks. Researchers in Dhaka (then East Pakistan) and Calcutta found that the intestine continues to absorb salt and water in cholera if glucose is present.

At the Cholera Research Laboratory in Dhaka, Richard Cash and David Nalin successfully tested an oral glucose–salt solution in 29 patients, publishing in The Lancet in 1968. In 1971, as refugees fled to India during the war that created Bangladesh, cholera broke out in the camps. Mahalanabis, of the Johns Hopkins centre in Calcutta, used drums of oral solution administered largely by family members, and the case fatality rate fell significantly.

In 1978 The Lancet called the discovery potentially the most important medical advance of the century. Even so, persuading sceptical clinicians that minimally trained people could give it took years.

title: Kangaroo mother care begins in Bogotá
summary: In 1978, faced with overcrowding and too few incubators, neonatologists Edgar Rey Sanabria and Héctor Martínez at Bogotá's Instituto Materno Infantil began keeping small and premature babies in continuous skin-to-skin contact with their mothers.
explanation:
The method has three parts: the baby is held upright against the mother's (or another carer's) bare chest, is breastfed, ideally exclusively, and goes home early with close follow-up. It was devised as an alternative to scarce and sometimes unsafe incubator care.

The idea spread from Colombia to Brazil and well beyond. Randomised trials followed: a Cochrane review of 21 studies including more than 3,000 low-birthweight infants found better growth with kangaroo care, and later reviews report lower mortality compared with standard care, particularly in low- and middle-income countries. WHO now recommends it for clinically stable newborns weighing 2,000 g or less.

Kangaroo care shows a pattern common in medicine: a practical solution from a resource-constrained setting, later confirmed by trials and adopted in wealthy countries too.

summary: In 1972 Graham Liggins and Ross Howie published the first randomised, placebo-controlled trial of giving corticosteroids to mothers at risk of preterm birth. Babies whose mothers received betamethasone had less respiratory distress and lower mortality.
explanation:
The idea came from sheep. Liggins, an obstetrician in Auckland, was infusing pregnant ewes with corticosteroids to study what triggers labour. One delivered a lamb so premature it should not have survived, yet it was breathing. Its lungs had matured faster than expected.

With the paediatrician Ross Howie, Liggins designed a double-blind trial at a tertiary obstetric hospital in Auckland: women at risk of preterm birth received betamethasone or a matching placebo. The steroid reduced neonatal respiratory distress syndrome and deaths, and appeared safe in the short term. Follow-up of the trial's children has continued for decades, into adulthood.

Antenatal corticosteroids became a cornerstone of care for threatened preterm birth worldwide, although adoption was slow for years after the trial, and questions about timing and dose are still being studied.

title: The first human heart transplant, Cape Town
summary: In the early hours of 3 December 1967, at Groote Schuur Hospital, a team led by Christiaan Barnard transplanted the heart of Denise Darvall, a 25-year-old killed in a road accident, into Louis Washkansky. He lived for 18 days.
explanation:
Barnard had established an open-heart surgery programme at Groote Schuur Hospital and the University of Cape Town in 1958. Several teams in the United States had prepared for heart transplantation through years of animal research and were close to attempting it.

Denise Darvall was struck by a car outside a bakery in Observatory, Cape Town, and declared brain dead. Her heart was transplanted into Louis Washkansky, a 54-year-old with severe heart failure, and was shocked into beating just before 6 a.m. on 3 December. He died 18 days later of pneumonia. Barnard's second patient, Philip Blaiberg, lived for about 19 months.

The operation drew worldwide attention, and surgeons elsewhere, including Euryclides Zerbini's team in Brazil, began preparing their own transplants within days.

title: Aro village system: psychiatric care in the community
summary: From the mid-1950s, the Nigerian psychiatrist Thomas Adeoye Lambo, at the new Aro hospital in Abeokuta, arranged for patients to live in nearby villages during treatment, working with local communities and traditional healers.
explanation:
The Aro Mental Hospital opened in Abeokuta in 1954, under the British colonial government. Lambo, Nigeria's first Indigenous psychiatrist, had trained in Britain, including at the Maudsley Hospital, and returned in 1952. Rather than confining patients in wards, he arranged for them to live in surrounding villages while attending the hospital for treatment.

The Aro village system built on existing community structures, gave the villages health clinics and infrastructure in return, and drew traditional healers into care. It also supported research, such as the Cornell–Aro project, showing that major psychiatric disorders occurred in Nigeria in ways comparable to elsewhere.

The approach became an influential example of culturally grounded community psychiatry and inspired rehabilitation villages in Tanzania from 1969. Lambo later became Deputy Director-General of the World Health Organization.

title: The first CT scan of a patient's brain
summary: On 1 October 1971 at Atkinson Morley's Hospital in London, a prototype scanner built by the EMI engineer Godfrey Hounsfield produced a cross-sectional X-ray image of a living patient's brain, revealing a tumour.
explanation:
Conventional X-rays superimpose everything in their path onto a single picture. Hounsfield, an engineer at EMI, conceived of taking many X-ray measurements from different angles and using a computer to reconstruct a slice through the body. EMI, flush with income from its music business, and the British Department of Health funded the work.

The prototype was installed at Atkinson Morley's Hospital, where the radiologist James Ambrose scanned the first patient on 1 October 1971: the image showed a cystic tumour in the frontal lobe, and the surgeon later confirmed it looked as the picture predicted. Each slice took minutes to acquire and longer to compute, but neurologists around the world quickly sought the new machines.

The physicist Allan Cormack had independently worked out the mathematics of reconstructing images from projections. He and Hounsfield shared the 1979 Nobel Prize.

title: Two IVF births in 1978: Oldham and Calcutta
summary: On 25 July 1978 Louise Brown was born in Oldham, England, after in vitro fertilisation by Robert Edwards, Patrick Steptoe and Jean Purdy. Sixty-seven days later, on 3 October, a team in Calcutta led by Subhas Mukhopadhyay announced the birth of Durga (Kanupriya Agarwal).
explanation:
Robert Edwards had pursued the idea of fertilising human eggs outside the body since the 1950s. With the gynaecologist Patrick Steptoe, who retrieved eggs by laparoscopy, and the embryologist and nurse Jean Purdy, he worked through years of experiments and failures. Louise Brown, born at Oldham General Hospital, was the first child conceived through IVF.

In Calcutta, Subhas Mukhopadhyay, with Sunit Mukherjee and the gynaecologist Saroj Kanti Bhattacharya, used a different approach, including ovarian stimulation, and announced the birth of Durga on 3 October 1978. Both announcements met scepticism. The British team went on to further births; Mukhopadhyay was transferred to an eye hospital and could not continue his work. Today his team's work is widely acknowledged as the world's second IVF birth.

IVF has since led to millions of births worldwide. Edwards received the Nobel Prize in 2010.

title: Polio vaccines tested on millions of children
summary: In 1954 about 1.8 million children in the United States, Canada and Finland took part in field trials of Jonas Salk's inactivated polio vaccine, announced as safe and effective on 12 April 1955. Albert Sabin's oral vaccine was then tested on a vast scale in the Soviet Union from 1958–59.
explanation:
Polio paralysed 13,000–20,000 people a year in the United States alone in the early 1950s. Salk, at the University of Pittsburgh, made a vaccine from killed poliovirus. The March of Dimes funded a field trial supervised by Thomas Francis Jr. of the University of Michigan: some children received vaccine or an injected placebo, with neither families nor officials knowing which, while others were observed as controls. On 12 April 1955 Francis announced that the vaccine was safe and effective, and it was licensed the same day.

Within weeks, two lots made by Cutter Laboratories turned out to contain live virus. Thousands of people received the faulty vaccine, and some developed paralysis.

Sabin's live, oral vaccine was tested instead, during the Cold War, in the Soviet Union, first on thousands and then on millions of children, before being adopted worldwide.

title: Ring vaccination trial against Ebola in Guinea
summary: During the 2013–16 West African Ebola epidemic, the Ebola ça Suffit! trial in Guinea vaccinated contacts, and contacts of contacts, of confirmed cases either immediately or after 21 days. No one vaccinated immediately developed Ebola from ten days onwards.
explanation:
Testing a vaccine during a fast-moving epidemic is difficult. The trial, run by Guinean authorities with WHO, Médecins Sans Frontières and other partners, used ring vaccination, the containment strategy that had helped eradicate smallpox. Each newly confirmed case defined a ring of contacts and contacts of contacts, and rings were randomly assigned to immediate or delayed vaccination with a single dose of rVSV-ZEBOV.

Among those vaccinated immediately there were no cases of Ebola with onset ten or more days after randomisation, while cases did occur in the delayed group. The final results, published in 2017, estimated vaccine efficacy at 100 per cent, with wide statistical uncertainty.

The vaccine was later used in further outbreaks and real-world studies found it highly effective. The trial showed that rigorous evaluation can be done in the middle of an emergency in a low-income country.

title: Alma-Ata declares primary health care the route to 'Health for All'
summary: On 12 September 1978, the International Conference on Primary Health Care in Alma-Ata, in the Kazakh Soviet Socialist Republic, adopted a declaration calling health a fundamental human right and primary health care the key to health for all.
explanation:
The conference, convened by WHO and UNICEF, brought together delegations from 134 countries. Its declaration defined health broadly, as complete physical, mental and social well-being, and called existing inequalities in health between and within countries politically, socially and economically unacceptable.

It set the goal of 'Health for All by the Year 2000' and argued that this could be reached through primary health care: essential, accessible care close to where people live and work, with community participation and action across sectors beyond health.

The goal was not met, and in the following years many programmes narrowed to selected interventions. But primary health care became a core concept for WHO, and in 2018 the Declaration of Astana, in the same country, reaffirmed Alma-Ata as the foundation for universal health coverage.

whatChanged: Put primary health care and health equity at the centre of global health policy.
whyItMattered: Shaped four decades of health-system planning and remains the reference point for universal health coverage.
limitations: A declaration is a commitment, not an outcome; 'Health for All by 2000' was not achieved.
Its broad vision was soon narrowed in practice to selected, targeted programmes in many countries.

title: The Human Genome Project publishes a draft, then a near-complete sequence
summary: An international consortium of 20 groups in six countries published a draft human genome sequence in 2001 and announced an essentially complete sequence in April 2003, two years ahead of schedule. It covered about 92% of the genome.
explanation:
The Human Genome Project began formally in 1990, when the US National Institutes of Health and Department of Energy published a plan for the first five years of an expected 15-year effort. Sequencing was carried out by the International Human Genome Sequencing Consortium: 20 groups in the United States, the United Kingdom, Japan, France, Germany and China. A draft was announced in June 2000 and published in Nature in February 2001, alongside a competing draft from the company Celera Genomics.

In April 2003 the consortium announced an essentially complete sequence, as complete as the sequencing technology of the time allowed. The project also changed scientific practice: the sequence was released publicly shortly after it was produced, under the 1996 Bermuda Principles on open data.

title: The last 8% of a human genome is sequenced
summary: In 2022 the Telomere-to-Telomere (T2T) Consortium published a complete, gapless 3.055-billion-base-pair sequence of a human genome. It covered every chromosome except Y, including the repetitive regions the Human Genome Project could not finish.
explanation:
The reference human genome released from 2000 onwards covered the gene-rich parts of the chromosomes but left about 8% unfinished: highly repetitive regions such as centromeres and the arrays of ribosomal DNA genes, which the short sequence reads of the time could not piece together. That missing 8% is comparable in size to a whole chromosome.

The T2T Consortium, led by researchers at the US National Human Genome Research Institute, the University of California, Santa Cruz, and the University of Washington, used newer long-read sequencing on a cell line that carries only one copy of each chromosome, which made the repeats easier to assemble. Their main paper, one of six in Science on 1 April 2022, reported gapless sequences for all chromosomes except Y, corrected errors in the earlier reference and added nearly 200 million base pairs of new sequence.

title: A portable pressure bag for altitude sickness
summary: Igor Gamow of the University of Colorado, Boulder, patented a lightweight, inflatable hyperbaric chamber in 1990. Pumped up around a climber, it simulates a lower altitude and is used to treat severe mountain sickness where descent is not possible.
explanation:
Severe altitude illness, including fluid on the lungs or brain, is treated by descending. When that is impossible, raising the air pressure around the patient has a similar effect. Gamow and Geoffrey Geer first patented a portable chamber for studying exercise at raised pressure; the design they patented in the United States in 1990 was a backpackable, inflatable bag about the size of a sleeping bag.

Portable hyperbaric bags are now recommended for severe mountain sickness when descent is risky. A case report from Mount Everest describes a climber with high-altitude pulmonary oedema treated in a Gamow bag for two hours at 7,060 m before descending safely.

whatChanged: Climbers with severe altitude illness could be treated on the mountain when bad weather, darkness or injury prevented descent.
whyItMattered: It gave expedition doctors a way to buy time in an emergency at altitude.
limitations: The bag is a temporary measure: descent remains the definitive treatment.
Evidence for its benefit comes mainly from case reports and small studies.

title: Brugada syndrome described as a cause of sudden cardiac death
summary: In 1992 Pedro and Josep Brugada described eight people who had survived sudden cardiac arrest despite structurally normal hearts, all sharing a distinctive ECG pattern. The condition, now called Brugada syndrome, is an inherited cause of sudden death.
explanation:
The Brugadas' multicentre report in the Journal of the American College of Cardiology described six men and two women with repeated episodes of aborted sudden death that no known disease explained. During normal rhythm their ECGs showed a right bundle branch block pattern with persistent ST-segment elevation in the right chest leads; the fatal rhythm was a rapid polymorphic ventricular tachycardia.

Naming the pattern made it possible to recognise people at risk from a routine ECG. Later research linked the syndrome to inherited faults in the genes for heart ion channels, and drugs such as ajmaline or flecainide came to be used to unmask concealed forms.

whatChanged: A specific ECG pattern could be linked to a high risk of sudden death in people with otherwise normal hearts.
whyItMattered: It explains some sudden deaths in young adults and children, and allows relatives and at-risk people to be screened and protected, for example with an implanted defibrillator.
limitations: Many people with the ECG pattern but no symptoms are at low risk, so deciding whom to treat remains difficult.
contested: Martini and colleagues had described patients with a similar ECG pattern and ventricular fibrillation in 1989, though they reported subtle structural abnormalities of the right ventricle.

title: Vaccines against hepatitis A are licensed
summary: An inactivated hepatitis A vaccine, Havrix, was licensed in Europe in 1991 after development involving GSK Biologicals in Belgium and US government laboratories. A live attenuated vaccine was licensed in China in 1992.
explanation:
Hepatitis A virus was identified by electron microscopy at the US National Institutes of Health, but a vaccine depended on growing it in cell cultures suitable for manufacture. Havrix, a formalin-inactivated vaccine, built on strain HM-175 and work in Robert Purcell's laboratory at the NIH, with human trials at the Walter Reed Army Institute of Research from 1986 and a phase 3 trial in Thailand. It was developed by SmithKline Beecham Biologicals at Rixensart, Belgium, licensed in Europe in 1991 and in the United States in 1995.

China took a different route: a live attenuated vaccine based on the H2 strain was licensed there in 1992. Vaccination of children in several countries has since been followed by large falls in hepatitis A.

title: Injecting a single sperm into an egg: ICSI in Brussels
summary: In 1992 a team at the Free University of Brussels reported pregnancies and births after injecting a single sperm directly into a human egg. Intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI) became the standard treatment for severe male infertility.
explanation:
In-vitro fertilisation often failed when sperm were few or poorly motile. The Brussels Centre for Reproductive Medicine, headed by André Van Steirteghem and Paul Devroey, had been placing sperm under the egg's outer coat (subzonal insemination). The team, including Gianpiero Palermo, also began injecting a sperm directly into some eggs, and found fertilisation much more consistent that way; a pregnancy from such an embryo in April 1991 led to a birth on 14 January 1992.

They abandoned the older method and reported in The Lancet in July 1992: of 47 eggs injected, 31 fertilised, and four pregnancies resulted, with four healthy babies delivered.

limitations: Earlier attempts at microinjection had been made elsewhere with little success.
Follow-up studies monitor genetic and developmental outcomes, since some causes of male infertility can be passed on.

title: Dolly the sheep is cloned from an adult cell
summary: Dolly, born at the Roslin Institute near Edinburgh on 5 July 1996, was the first mammal cloned from a fully specialised adult cell. Her birth showed that an adult cell's DNA could still direct the development of a whole animal.
explanation:
Earlier experiments had cloned amphibians, and the Roslin team had cloned the sheep Megan and Morag from cultured embryo cells in 1995. Many believed that fully specialised adult cells could not be reprogrammed in this way. Ian Wilmut, Keith Campbell and colleagues used somatic cell nuclear transfer, placing the nucleus of an udder cell from a six-year-old Finn Dorset ewe into an egg cell, and transferred the resulting embryo to a surrogate.

Dolly's birth was announced in February 1997 with the publication of 'Viable offspring derived from fetal and adult mammalian cells' in Nature. The experiment is widely seen as a stepping stone from earlier amphibian cloning to the reprogramming of adult human cells into stem cells.

whatChanged: It showed that the genetic material of specialised adult cells can be reprogrammed to produce a complete animal.
whyItMattered: It overturned a central assumption of developmental biology and opened the path to reprogramming adult cells for regenerative medicine, while prompting wide ethical debate about cloning.
limitations: Dolly was one success among many failed attempts, and cloning remains inefficient.
Dolly was not the first cloned mammal: sheep had been cloned from embryo cells before.

title: Human embryonic stem cells are grown in the laboratory
summary: In November 1998 James Thomson's team at the University of Wisconsin–Madison reported five lines of human embryonic stem cells, derived from donated IVF embryos. The cells could multiply indefinitely and form tissues of all three germ layers.
explanation:
James Thomson, chief pathologist at the Wisconsin Regional Primate Research Center, began work on embryonic stem cells in 1995. His team took the inner cell mass from human blastocysts, embryos a few days old donated by couples who had undergone IVF, and established five cell lines with normal chromosomes and high telomerase activity. The cells could form tissues of all three germ layers, including gut lining, cartilage, bone, muscle and nerve tissue.

A team led by John Gearhart published a related method from germ cells shortly afterwards. Human embryonic stem cells became a major tool for studying development and testing drugs, and the basis for experimental cell therapies.

whatChanged: Human cells able to become any tissue could be grown and studied in quantity.
whyItMattered: It opened research into human development, disease modelling and cell replacement, and led to sustained public debate over the use of human embryos.
limitations: Deriving the cells destroys the embryo, which has made the research ethically and politically contested.
Treatments based on the cells have been slow to reach patients.

title: Ghrelin, a hunger hormone from the stomach, is identified
summary: In 1999 Masayasu Kojima, Kenji Kangawa and colleagues in Osaka identified ghrelin, a 28-amino-acid peptide made in the stomach. It releases growth hormone and turned out to stimulate appetite.
explanation:
Synthetic drugs had been found to release growth hormone through a receptor whose natural signal was unknown. Kangawa's group at the National Cardiovascular Center Research Institute in Suita, Osaka, purified the missing natural signal from rat stomach. It was a peptide of 28 amino acids with an unusual fatty-acid modification, and they named it ghrelin.

Later work showed that ghrelin also stimulates appetite, earning it the nickname 'hunger hormone'. It has since been studied in obesity, wasting and heart failure.

whyItMattered: It changed understanding of how appetite and energy balance are regulated and opened new lines of research on obesity and wasting.
limitations: The original discovery was made in rats; the hormone's role in human appetite was established by later studies.
Drugs targeting ghrelin have had limited clinical success so far.

title: A swallowable camera pill images the small bowel
summary: In 2000 Gavriel Iddan of Given Imaging in Israel and Paul Swain of the Royal London Hospital described a wireless capsule endoscope: a pill containing a camera, light and transmitter that photographs the gut as it passes through.
explanation:
Most of the small intestine was hard to reach with conventional endoscopes. Iddan, an electro-optical engineer, began working on a swallowable camera in Israel in the early 1990s, while Swain pursued similar ideas in London; the two groups joined forces from 1998, and Given Imaging was founded in Yokneam to develop the device. Swain was the first person to swallow it, in October 1999.

The team reported the device in Nature in May 2000, and in January 2001 published the first images of disease in the human small bowel taken with it, in patients with unexplained bleeding.

whatChanged: The whole small intestine could be examined without sedation or a flexible tube.

title: Surgeons in New York operate on a patient in Strasbourg
summary: On 7 September 2001 Jacques Marescaux's team in New York removed the gallbladder of a patient in Strasbourg using a surgical robot controlled over a transatlantic high-speed link. The 'Lindbergh operation' showed that long-distance surgery was technically feasible.
explanation:
Keyhole surgery already put a screen between surgeon and patient. The question was whether that distance could be thousands of kilometres without a dangerous delay between the surgeon's movement and the robot's response. Marescaux's institute in Strasbourg, IRCAD, founded in 1994 to link surgery and computing, set out to reduce that delay using the Zeus surgical robot and a high-speed telecommunications link.

The patient, fully informed, was operated on under general anaesthesia at Strasbourg's university hospital while the surgeons worked in New York. The operation was reported in Nature that month.

whatChanged: A complete operation was shown to be possible with the surgeon on another continent.
whyItMattered: It demonstrated that a surgeon could operate across an ocean, a step towards bringing specialist surgery to places without specialist surgeons.
limitations: It was a single demonstration on one patient; it did not by itself make remote surgery routine.

title: Carlo Urbani raises the alarm over SARS in Hanoi
summary: In February–March 2003 Carlo Urbani, a WHO infectious disease specialist in Hanoi, recognised that a pneumonia spreading through the French Hospital was a new and dangerous disease. His warnings helped trigger isolation measures and a global alert. He died of SARS on 29 March 2003.
explanation:
A businessman with a high fever was admitted to the French Hospital in Hanoi on 26 February 2003. Urbani, asked to help on 28 February, saw hospital staff falling ill and concluded that this was a new and highly contagious disease. He alerted WHO headquarters and persuaded Vietnamese health officials to isolate patients, cordon off the hospital and screen travellers.

On 15 March WHO declared the disease Urbani had identified a worldwide health threat. Urbani developed symptoms on 11 March on a flight to Bangkok, and died there on 29 March after nearly three weeks in isolation. Viet Nam's quick containment of its outbreak is credited to resolute government action and to his early work.

title: Face transplants: partial in Amiens, full in Barcelona
summary: In November 2005 surgeons in Amiens, France, transplanted the nose, lips and chin of a brain-dead donor onto Isabelle Dinoire, who had been disfigured in an animal attack. In March 2010 a team in Barcelona performed the first full face transplant.
explanation:
Transplanting a face, a composite of skin, muscle, nerves and sometimes bone, was debated for years because it requires lifelong immunosuppression for a procedure that is not life-saving. After the French national ethics committee accepted partial transplants while expressing reservations about full ones, Bernard Devauchelle and Jean-Michel Dubernard led the Amiens operation on 27 November 2005; Dubernard had performed the first hand transplant of the modern era in 1998.

Further partial transplants followed in China, France and the United States. In March 2010 a team led by Joan Pere Barret at Vall d'Hebron University Hospital in Barcelona replaced a man's whole face in one piece.

title: A vaccine against the virus behind cervical cancer
summary: Ian Frazer and Jian Zhou at the University of Queensland made virus-like particles that mimic human papillomavirus (HPV) from 1991. The technology led to Gardasil, approved in Australia and the United States in 2006 to prevent infection with the HPV types that cause most cervical cancers.
explanation:
Certain HPV types cause cervical cancer; types 16 and 18 alone cause about 70% of cases. The live virus could not be grown in the laboratory to make a conventional vaccine. Frazer, an immunologist in Brisbane, met the virologist Jian Zhou in Cambridge in 1989 and invited him to Queensland. With Xiao-Yi Sun and others they produced HPV surface proteins that self-assembled into empty, non-infectious shells resembling the virus, which provoke a strong antibody response.

In 1995 the technology was licensed through CSL to Merck, whose vaccine Gardasil, covering HPV types 6, 11, 16 and 18, was approved in 2006; GSK's Cervarix, also based on virus-like particles, followed. Zhou died in 1999, before the vaccine reached use.

title: Rotavirus vaccines return after an early setback
summary: The original rotavirus vaccine, RotaShield, was withdrawn in 1999 after it was linked to a rare bowel blockage. Two new oral vaccines, RotaTeq and Rotarix, were each tested in 60,000–70,000 infants and introduced from 2006.
explanation:
Rotavirus causes severe diarrhoea in young children, some of whom become dangerously dehydrated. RotaShield, licensed in the United States in 1998, was withdrawn in 1999 when surveillance linked it to intussusception, a bowel blockage, in about 1 in 10,000 vaccinated infants.

The next vaccines were tested in exceptionally large trials designed to detect such a risk. RotaTeq, a bovine–human reassortant vaccine developed by H. Fred Clark, Stanley Plotkin and Paul Offit, was licensed in the United States in February 2006. Rotarix, an attenuated human strain from GSK, was reported effective in a large trial published the same year and licensed in the United States in 2008. Both are given as drops by mouth.

locationNote: Both vaccines were tested in multinational trials and introduced in many countries; no single place is mapped.

whatChanged: Infants could be protected against severe rotavirus diarrhoea with oral vaccines whose safety had been tested in very large trials.
whyItMattered: Both vaccines are now recommended for use worldwide, protecting infants against a major cause of severe childhood diarrhoea.
limitations: A small increased risk of intussusception has been found after both newer vaccines, judged to be outweighed by their benefits.

title: An approved retinal implant restores some sight
summary: The Argus II retinal prosthesis, developed by Second Sight in California from work begun at Johns Hopkins, received European approval in 2011 and US approval in 2013. It gave some people blinded by retinitis pigmentosa limited, artificial vision.
explanation:
In retinitis pigmentosa the light-sensing cells of the retina die, but other retinal nerve cells survive. The Argus II stimulates those surviving cells with an array of 60 electrodes implanted on the retina.

The device received the CE mark in Europe in 2011 and US approval as a humanitarian use device in February 2013, after a trial in 30 patients. It was the first visual prosthesis to become commercially available; more than 350 people had been implanted by 2019.

people.name: Mark Humayun and Robert Greenberg
people.role: Began developing a retinal prosthesis at Johns Hopkins University

whatChanged: Some people with profound blindness from retinal degeneration could perceive light, shapes and movement again.
whyItMattered: It showed that an electronic implant could provide useful, if limited, vision, and established a path for later visual prostheses.
limitations: The vision provided is crude and far from normal sight.
US approval was as a humanitarian use device, which did not require proof of effectiveness.
In 2019 the company announced that it would concentrate on a brain implant instead.

title: Uterus transplants lead to births
summary: In 2011 surgeons in Antalya, Turkey, transplanted a uterus from a deceased donor, and the recipient later became pregnant. In 2014 a woman in Gothenburg, Sweden, gave birth after receiving a uterus from a living donor, the first live birth after uterus transplantation.
explanation:
Women born without a uterus or who have lost it could not carry a pregnancy. After a failed attempt in Jeddah, Saudi Arabia, in 2000 and years of animal research, a team at Akdeniz University Hospital in Antalya led by Ömer Özkan carried out a transplant from a deceased donor in 2011, and the recipient later became pregnant.

In Sweden, Mats Brännström's team at Sahlgrenska University Hospital began a trial of transplants from living donors in 2012. In 2014 one recipient, a 35-year-old woman born without a uterus, gave birth to a healthy boy, reported in The Lancet as proof of concept.

people.name: Ömer Özkan
people.role: Plastic surgeon; led the Antalya team

whatChanged: Women with absolute uterine-factor infertility could carry their own pregnancy.
whyItMattered: It created a new option for a form of infertility previously treatable only by adoption or surrogacy.
limitations: The procedures involve major surgery for donor and recipient and temporary immunosuppression.
Numbers remain small; the first birth from a deceased-donor uterus was reported in Brazil only in 2017.

title: Growing organs in the laboratory: kidney, liver and heart
summary: In 2013 teams in Boston and Yokohama grew a working rat kidney on a stripped-down organ scaffold and a vascularised human liver bud from stem cells. In 2019 a team in Tel Aviv 3D-printed a small heart from a patient's own cells. None has yet been used in patients.
explanation:
The shortage of donor organs has driven efforts to build organs in the laboratory. At Massachusetts General Hospital, Harald Ott's team washed the cells out of rat kidneys, leaving a collagen scaffold, repopulated it with new cells and transplanted the result into rats, where it produced urine. At Yokohama City University, Takanori Takebe and Hideki Taniguchi's team grew 'liver buds' from human induced pluripotent stem cells that connected to the blood supply when transplanted into mice and rescued them from liver failure.

In 2019 Tal Dvir's group at Tel Aviv University printed a heart the size of a rabbit's, with blood vessels and chambers, from fatty tissue taken from patients.

date.basis: Kidney and liver studies published in April and July 2013; printed heart announced in April 2019.

whatChanged: Laboratory-built organ tissue was shown to connect to a living blood supply and perform some organ functions in animals.
whyItMattered: These proofs of concept point towards organs made to order from a patient's own cells, which would avoid both donor shortages and rejection.
limitations: All three were laboratory or animal studies; none produced an organ used in a person.
Producing such tissue in the quantities needed for human transplantation was not yet possible.

title: A 3D-printed implant replaces the top of a skull
summary: Surgeons at University Medical Center Utrecht replaced most of the skull of a 22-year-old woman, whose bone had thickened to compress her brain, with a custom 3D-printed plastic implant. The 23-hour operation was announced in March 2014.
explanation:
The patient had a rare condition in which her skull kept thickening, to about 5 cm, causing headaches, loss of vision and poor coordination. Skull defects had previously been repaired with cement shaped by hand during surgery. Led by the neurosurgeon Bon Verweij, the Utrecht team removed the top of her skull and fitted a plastic implant printed to the exact shape of her head by the Australian company Anatomics.

The hospital waited three months before announcing the operation in March 2014, by which time the patient was symptom-free and back at work.

title: An 'artificial pancreas' adjusts insulin automatically
summary: In September 2016 the US FDA approved Medtronic's MiniMed 670G, the first hybrid closed-loop system for type 1 diabetes. A sensor measures glucose every five minutes and a pump adjusts background insulin automatically.
explanation:
People with type 1 diabetes must constantly check their glucose and dose insulin, usually with injections or a pump that they program themselves. A system in which a glucose sensor automatically controls an insulin pump, a 'closed loop', is often called an artificial pancreas.

The MiniMed 670G was approved on 28 September 2016 for people aged 14 and over, after a study of 123 participants. It measures glucose every five minutes and automatically sets background (basal) insulin; users still give mealtime doses themselves, which is why it is called a hybrid system and was seen as a step towards a fully closed loop.

date.basis: Date of FDA approval.

locationNote: A regulatory approval of a device tested at several centres; no single place is mapped.
whatChanged: Part of the work of managing type 1 diabetes, adjusting background insulin day and night, could be handed to an automated system.
whyItMattered: It was the first approved system to hand part of insulin dosing to an automated controller.
limitations: Users still had to count carbohydrates and give mealtime doses.
Approval was based on a three-month study of 123 people.
'First' refers to approval by the US regulator, not to the first closed-loop system ever built or tested.

title: The pressurised metered-dose asthma inhaler
summary: In 1956 Riker Laboratories in Los Angeles introduced the first pressurised metered-dose inhaler, prompted by a 13-year-old with asthma who asked why her medicine could not come in a spray can like hairspray.
explanation:
Before the inhaler, many people with asthma used fragile glass squeeze-bulb nebulisers. In 1955 Susie Maison asked her father George Maison, president of Riker Laboratories, a subsidiary of the Rexall drug company, whether her medicine could be delivered like aerosol hairspray. Riker's chemists Irving Porush and Charles Thiel, drawing on advice from Rexall's cosmetics laboratory, formulated asthma drugs with a propellant in a small pressurised canister with a valve that released a measured dose.

The device was approved by the US Food and Drug Administration in March 1956 and marketed as the Medihaler. Pocket inhalers built on the same principle became the standard way of taking asthma medicines.

whatChanged: People with asthma could carry a small device that delivered a measured dose of medicine directly to the lungs.
whyItMattered: The metered-dose inhaler became the most common way to take asthma medicines and has been used by hundreds of millions of people.
limitations: Early inhalers used CFC refrigerant propellants.
The inventors' story comes largely from later interviews and award citations.
'First' refers to the first pressurised metered-dose inhaler; inhaled asthma drugs had earlier been given with fragile glass nebulisers.

title: Ultrasound is used to look inside the abdomen and womb
summary: In June 1958 Ian Donald, John MacVicar and engineer Tom Brown in Glasgow reported using pulsed ultrasound to examine more than 100 patients, including pregnant women. Their team went on to build the first commercial ultrasound scanner, the Diasonograph, in 1963.
explanation:
Ian Donald, Regius Professor of Midwifery at the University of Glasgow, had seen industrial ultrasound flaw detectors used to find cracks in metal and wondered whether echoes could distinguish tissues in the body. Working with the obstetrician John MacVicar at the Western Infirmary and Tom Brown of the instrument makers Kelvin & Hughes, he built prototype scanners.

Their paper in The Lancet, 'Investigation of abdominal masses by pulsed ultrasound', showed images of ovarian cysts, fibroids and a fetal skull. The team's Diasonograph of 1963 was the first commercial ultrasound scanner, and ultrasound became a routine part of pregnancy care.

whyItMattered: Obstetric ultrasound became one of the most widely used imaging tests in medicine, used to date pregnancies, monitor growth and detect abnormalities.
limitations: The early machines were very large: the Diasonograph weighed about a tonne.
'First commercial scanner' refers to the Diasonograph; the same team had built earlier prototypes over nearly a decade.

title: A pacemaker is implanted in a patient's body
summary: On 8 October 1958, at the Karolinska Hospital in Stockholm, the surgeon Åke Senning implanted a pacemaker built by the engineer Rune Elmqvist into Arne Larsson, a 43-year-old whose heart condition had become critical.
explanation:
Senning and Elmqvist, who worked for the company Elema-Schönander, were developing a fully implantable pacemaker but did not think it was ready for human use. Arne Larsson's heart condition had become life-threatening, and his wife Else-Marie, who had read about the experimental device in a newspaper, persuaded them to try it.

The first device was damaged during the operation and stopped working after the first night; an identical second device was implanted the next day, and Larsson's life was saved. Implantable pacemakers became a standard treatment for slow or blocked heart rhythms.

date.basis: Date of the operation, reported consistently by the manufacturer and historians.

whatChanged: A heart with a failing natural rhythm could be paced by a device carried entirely inside the body.
whyItMattered: Implantable pacemakers have since been fitted in millions of people, and the technology underlies implantable defibrillators.
limitations: The first device worked only for hours; reliable long-lasting pacemakers took years to develop.
Other teams implanted pacemakers soon afterwards, including in Uruguay in 1960, and several groups share credit for the technology.

title: IVF works in a mammal: rabbits born from eggs fertilised in a dish
summary: In 1959 Min Chueh Chang at the Worcester Foundation in Massachusetts fertilised black rabbits' eggs with black rabbits' sperm in the laboratory and transferred them to a white female, which gave birth to black young. It showed that in-vitro fertilisation could produce live offspring.
explanation:
Chang, a reproductive biologist who had joined Gregory Pincus at the Worcester Foundation for Experimental Biology in 1945, designed an experiment whose result could not be mistaken: black offspring born to a white surrogate could only have come from black rabbits' eggs fertilised in the dish.

Chang went on to study in-vitro fertilisation in hamsters, mice and rats. His work helped form the basis for human IVF by Robert Edwards and Patrick Steptoe, which led to the birth of Louise Brown in 1978. He also contributed to the development of the contraceptive pill.

locations.name: Worcester Foundation for Experimental Biology, Shrewsbury

limitations: It was an animal experiment; human IVF required nearly two more decades of work by others.

title: Mapping the brain's electrical activity across the scalp
summary: William Grey Walter used EEG with many small scalp electrodes to locate a brain tumour in 1936, and at the Burden Neurological Institute in Bristol in 1957 built the toposcope, which displayed brain electrical activity from many points at once.
explanation:
Hans Berger's electrodes were too large to show where in the brain activity came from. Working in London in 1936, Grey Walter showed that with many small electrodes and triangulation he could locate abnormal slow waves and so detect a cerebral tumour. Moving to the new Burden Neurological Institute in Bristol in 1939, he built a series of instruments to analyse the EEG.

His toposcope of 1957 arranged display tubes in a two-dimensional array matching the electrodes on the head, so that changing patterns of activity could be watched across the brain's surface.

locationNote: The 1936 tumour work was done in London, at the Maudsley Hospital's laboratory; the toposcope was built in Bristol.

title: Chest compressions and rescue breathing become CPR
summary: In 1960 William Kouwenhoven, James Jude and Guy Knickerbocker at Johns Hopkins reported that pressing rhythmically on the chest could keep blood flowing during cardiac arrest. Combined with Peter Safar's mouth-to-mouth breathing, it became modern cardiopulmonary resuscitation.
explanation:
Kouwenhoven, an electrical engineer, was developing a closed-chest defibrillator at Johns Hopkins. During experiments on dogs, the team found that pressure on the sternum could keep enough blood circulating to the brain. With the surgeon James Jude they refined the technique and reported in 1960 that closed-chest cardiac massage had been used in 20 patients in hospital, 14 of whom survived.

Meanwhile Peter Safar and James Elam had shown in experiments on volunteers that mouth-to-mouth breathing ventilated the lungs better than the manual methods then in use. Safar, Kouwenhoven and Jude combined the two into CPR, which could be learned easily and done without equipment.

locationNote: Safar's rescue-breathing studies were done at Baltimore City Hospitals, in the same city.
whatChanged: Anyone trained could keep oxygenated blood flowing to the brain after cardiac arrest until a defibrillator or other help arrived.
whyItMattered: CPR became the basis of resuscitation training worldwide and of the chain of survival for cardiac arrest.
limitations: Closed-chest massage had been described in the nineteenth century but abandoned in favour of opening the chest.

title: The contraceptive pill is approved
summary: In 1960 the US Food and Drug Administration approved Enovid, a hormonal pill developed by Gregory Pincus, Min Chueh Chang and John Rock, for contraception. Its approval rested largely on trials in Puerto Rico whose ethics have long been questioned.
explanation:
The birth-control campaigner Margaret Sanger and the philanthropist Katharine McCormick recruited Gregory Pincus of the Worcester Foundation to develop a hormonal contraceptive. Pincus and Min Chueh Chang experimented with synthetic progestins, and the gynaecologist John Rock gave synthetic progesterone to fifty women in Boston, whose ovulation stopped during treatment.

Because anti-contraception laws in Massachusetts and other states blocked large studies, the main trials began in 1956 in Río Piedras, Puerto Rico, followed by trials in Haiti and Mexico City. The FDA first approved Enovid in 1957 for menstrual disorders and then, in 1960, for contraception.

people.name: Edris Rice-Wray
people.role: Physician who ran the Puerto Rico trials day to day

whatChanged: Women gained a reliable contraceptive that they controlled themselves, separate from sex.
whyItMattered: The pill changed family planning, women's education and work, and social life across much of the world.
limitations: Enovid was first approved in 1957 only for menstrual disorders.
Some trial participants reported side effects.
harms: The large trials recruited poor women from a public housing project in Puerto Rico, a US territory. Participants consented, but critics have alleged that they were treated as guinea pigs, and local people questioned whether it was appropriate for outsiders to recruit women living in poverty.

title: Charnley's low-friction hip replacement
summary: In November 1962 John Charnley began using a hip replacement at Wrightington Hospital in Lancashire that combined a small polished metal ball with a high-density polyethylene socket, fixed with bone cement. It became the model for modern hip replacement.
explanation:
Earlier artificial hips often failed quickly. Charnley, an orthopaedic surgeon from Manchester, studied the friction of joint surfaces and moved his practice to a hip surgery centre at Wrightington Hospital in 1962. His first sockets of PTFE (Teflon) wore badly, so he switched to high-density polyethylene, which wore far more slowly.

He fixed the parts to bone with acrylic cement and used a clean-air enclosure in the operating theatre to reduce infection. Between November 1962 and 2005 more than 22,000 of his operations were performed at Wrightington alone.

limitations: Wear and loosening of the plastic socket remained the main long-term problems.

title: Beta blockers: propranolol for heart disease
summary: At ICI's laboratories at Alderley Park, Cheshire, James Black and colleagues set out to block the effect of adrenaline on the heart. After an earlier compound, pronethalol, they developed propranolol, introduced in the mid-1960s and the first widely successful beta blocker.
explanation:
Black set out to protect the heart by blocking the beta receptors through which adrenaline acts on it, building on Raymond Ahlquist's work on adrenaline receptors. Joining ICI Pharmaceuticals in 1958, he worked with the chemist John Stephenson and others. They derived propranolol from earlier compounds, dichloroisoprenaline and pronethalol; it was patented in 1962.

Propranolol revolutionised the treatment of ischaemic heart disease and was later used widely for high blood pressure. Black went on to develop cimetidine for stomach ulcers, and shared the 1988 Nobel Prize for his approach to designing drugs.

title: A balloon catheter removes blood clots without opening the artery
summary: Thomas Fogarty, while a medical student in Cincinnati around 1960, devised a thin catheter with a small balloon at the tip that could be passed beyond a clot, inflated and pulled back to drag the clot out. Reported in 1963, it began catheter-based treatment of blood vessels.
explanation:
Fogarty, who had worked as a surgical scrub technician at Good Samaritan Hospital in Cincinnati, saw that the existing operations to remove clots from arteries often failed. As a medical student he designed a thin catheter with a balloon at its tip. Introduced through a small cut, the deflated balloon was pushed past the clot, inflated, and withdrawn, pulling the clot out.

With the vascular surgeon Jack Cranley, Fogarty first used it in a patient in the early 1960s and published the method in 1963. Surgeons were initially sceptical, because touching the inside of a vessel was thought to cause clotting.

title: Liver transplantation: first attempts and first success
summary: Thomas Starzl attempted the first human liver transplants in Denver in 1963, but the early operations did not succeed. In 1967 he achieved the first successful liver transplant, at the University of Colorado.
explanation:
The liver's complexity and the strength of rejection made it far harder to transplant than the kidney. Starzl, who had built an active kidney transplant programme at the University of Colorado and the Denver Veterans Administration Hospital, performed the first human liver transplants in 1963, using azathioprine and steroids to control rejection.

In 1967 Starzl's team carried out the first successful liver transplant. He later helped bring the immunosuppressants cyclosporine and tacrolimus into transplant practice, which made liver transplants far more reliable.

title: The first human lung transplant, in Jackson, Mississippi
summary: On 11 June 1963 James Hardy's team at the University of Mississippi Medical Center transplanted a lung into John Russell, a 58-year-old prisoner with lung cancer. Russell lived 18 days and died of kidney failure.
explanation:
James Hardy's medical school dean granted him permission to attempt a human lung transplant under agreed conditions. John Russell, serving a life sentence at the Mississippi State Penitentiary, had a tumour blocking his left main airway and emphysema in his right lung. He received the left lung of a patient who had died of a heart attack.

The new lung worked, but Russell died 18 days later of kidney failure. The first lung transplant with long-term success came only in 1983.

title: Benzodiazepines: Librium and Valium
summary: Leo Sternbach at Hoffmann-La Roche in Nutley, New Jersey, discovered the first benzodiazepine, chlordiazepoxide (Librium), marketed in 1960. Diazepam (Valium) followed in 1963 and became one of the most prescribed drugs in the world.
explanation:
In the 1950s anxiety and insomnia were treated mainly with barbiturates. Sternbach, a chemist at Roche's US research centre, had set aside a family of compounds when a colleague tidying the laboratory found one that had never been tested. Submitted in 1957, it proved a potent calming drug and was marketed as Librium in 1960.

Roche's chemists modified the molecule to produce diazepam, introduced in 1963 as Valium. Benzodiazepines at first appeared less toxic and less likely to cause dependence than older drugs, and Valium was the best-selling medicine in the United States from 1968 until 1982.

whatChanged: Anxiety, insomnia, muscle spasm and seizures could be treated with drugs that at first appeared much safer than barbiturates.

limitations: Benzodiazepines proved more habit-forming than first thought, and Valium's use declined in the 1980s because of its addictive properties.

title: A measles vaccine is licensed
summary: John Enders and Thomas Peebles isolated measles virus in Boston in 1954 from a schoolboy, David Edmonston. Enders' team weakened it into a vaccine that was licensed in the United States in 1963; an improved version from 1968 is still used.
explanation:
Before the vaccine, nearly every American child caught measles by the age of 15, and it still killed about 500 Americans a year. During an outbreak at a boarding school near Boston in 1954, Peebles, a young paediatrician working with Enders at Boston Children's Hospital, collected samples; the virus from David Edmonston was grown in cell culture and gradually weakened.

The Edmonston-B vaccine was tested in small groups of children from 1958 and then in larger trials in New York and Nigeria. It was licensed in March 1963, but often caused fever and rash; Maurice Hilleman of Merck produced a further-weakened version in 1968, the only measles vaccine used in the United States since.

title: Cochlear implants bring sound to deaf people
summary: William House and John Doyle implanted the first cochlear electrodes in Los Angeles in 1961. House's single-channel device, made with 3M, became in 1984 the first cochlear implant approved by the US FDA for adults.
explanation:
Cochlear implants stimulate the auditory nerve electrically, bypassing the damaged inner ear. After reading of earlier attempts in France, the otologist William House, with the neurosurgeon John Doyle and engineer James Doyle, implanted electrodes in three patients in 1961. Working with the engineer Jack Urban from the mid-1960s, House developed a wearable device with an induction coil that passed signals through the skin, used from 1972.

Many researchers doubted that a single electrode could be useful, but more than 1,000 adults received the House device, and a trial in the late 1970s found implants beneficial. Multichannel implants, developed by teams including Blair Simmons's in California and Claude-Henri Chouard's in Paris, later became the standard.

title: A portable defibrillator takes heart-attack care to the patient
summary: In 1966 Frank Pantridge and John Geddes of the Royal Victoria Hospital, Belfast, launched a mobile coronary care unit: an ambulance carrying a doctor and a portable defibrillator to treat cardiac arrest before patients reached hospital.
explanation:
Pantridge had opened a coronary care unit in Belfast in late 1963, but argued that such units would be of little value if patients died before reaching hospital. With Geddes and the engineer John Anderson, he built a defibrillator that could run from a car battery; the first version, in 1965, weighed about 70 kg.

From 1966 a team travelled from the Royal Victoria Hospital to patients at the request of their family doctors. A 1967 editorial in The Lancet said that Pantridge and Geddes had revolutionised emergency medicine, and by 1968 Pantridge had a version weighing 3 kg. The 'Pantridge plan' was copied in many countries and led to the automated external defibrillator.

summary: On 16–17 December 1966 William Kelly and Richard Lillehei at the University of Minnesota transplanted a pancreas together with a kidney into a 28-year-old woman with diabetic kidney failure. People with type 1 diabetes depend on injected insulin and often develop kidney failure. Kelly and Lillehei transplanted part of a pancreas and a kidney from a deceased donor into a 28-year-old woman with kidney failure; for the first time, a person with type 1 diabetes became independent of insulin.

The University of Minnesota went on to perform more than 1,000 pancreas transplants, and outcomes improved with better immunosuppression. More than 50,000 pancreas transplants have since been performed worldwide.

title: Coronary bypass surgery with a leg vein
summary: On 9 May 1967 the Argentine surgeon René Favaloro, working at the Cleveland Clinic, used a segment of the patient's saphenous vein to carry blood past a blocked coronary artery. Coronary artery bypass grafting became one of the most common heart operations.
explanation:
Favaloro had studied thousands of the coronary angiograms made by Mason Sones at the Cleveland Clinic, which showed exactly where arteries were blocked. Earlier surgeons had experimented with other approaches, and Vasilii Kolesov in Leningrad had performed internal thoracic artery bypasses from 1964. Favaloro's systematic use of vein grafts from the leg, guided by angiography, made the operation reproducible.

He performed 13 more operations by October 1967 and published his results in 1968; by 1970 he and his colleagues had carried out more than 1,000.

title: Rubella vaccines protect unborn babies
summary: After a rubella epidemic in 1964–65 left thousands of American babies with birth defects, vaccines were developed by Harry Meyer and Paul Parkman at the US National Institutes of Health and by Stanley Plotkin at the Wistar Institute. The first were licensed in 1969.
explanation:
Rubella is usually mild, but infection in early pregnancy can cause miscarriage or congenital rubella syndrome, with damage to the heart, eyes, ears and brain. An epidemic in Europe in 1962–63 spread to the United States in 1964–65.

Parkman, who had helped isolate the virus at the Walter Reed Army Institute of Research, and Meyer at the NIH's Division of Biologics Standards weakened a strain, HPV-77, which was among three vaccines licensed in the United States in 1969. At the Wistar Institute in Philadelphia, Plotkin developed the RA 27/3 strain in human cells; licensed in the UK in 1972 and in the US in 1979, it is the basis of most rubella vaccines, including MMR, today.

title: Controlled-release drugs and the first skin patch
summary: Alejandro Zaffaroni founded ALZA in Palo Alto in 1968 to release drugs at a steady, controlled rate. After an eye insert for glaucoma in 1974, ALZA's scopolamine patch for motion sickness became in 1981 the first transdermal drug patch approved in the United States.
explanation:
Pills and injections deliver drugs in peaks and troughs. Zaffaroni, a chemist who had co-founded Syntex, founded ALZA to release drugs at a controlled rate, and filed for a patent on a transdermal system in 1969. Its first approved product, in 1974, was Ocusert, a thin film placed in the eye that released the glaucoma drug pilocarpine.

Working with Ciba-Geigy, ALZA gained approval for Transderm Scop in August 1981, followed two months later by a nitroglycerin patch for angina. Patches for nicotine and pain relief followed.
